annotations.text: Counter at 1440 — a second design, not a reflow

THE TWO-DESIGNS LAW, APPLIED

The house rule for the staff app is that 820px is a SWITCH between two designs. It holds here, and for a sharper reason: the desktop customer is a DIFFERENT PERSON. A bursar, a procurement officer, a contractor's office — someone with a keyboard, a printer and an approval to justify.

So the desktop is not the phone stretched. It earns its width three ways:

1. The account never leaves the screen. Balance, terms and remaining limit sit in the chrome on every page.
2. The catalogue sits BESIDE the order. On the phone, checking your order means leaving the catalogue; here the total moves as you type.
3. The statement gets its real columns — date, reference, detail, charge, payment, balance — and becomes a document somebody can print and file.

Same tokens, same ledger row, same one-action law. Body stays 15px: this is a customer, not a staff console, and nothing here is worth cramming.

WHAT THE THIRD TILE IS FOR

The phone shows two figures: what you owe, what your limit is. The desktop adds a third — what you have bought this year.

It is the only figure on the surface that is not about money owed, and it is there on purpose. A customer looking at 31,480,000 across 34 orders is looking at the case for asking you for better terms — and at the reason it would be tedious to start again somewhere else.

One strip, hairline dividers, no per-tile borders. Borrowed from the staff console because that part was already right.

THE ORDER PANE IS THE WHOLE ARGUMENT FOR DESKTOP

Every row carries its own stepper, so building a twenty-line order is twenty taps in one place rather than twenty round trips through an item screen.

The advice block rides in the pane, where the total is, so "you have no nails on this order" is read at the moment the number is being judged.

Out-of-stock keeps its row and offers "Tell me when it lands" rather than vanishing. A catalogue that hides what it hasn't got teaches customers to look elsewhere first.

THE GATE IS A DOOR, NOT A WALL

Everything in this product sits behind four figures typed on a phone, so the PIN screen decides whether the portal is used at all.

It goes on WhatsApp, not SMS — that channel already exists in the shop, it costs nothing per message, and it is where these customers already are.

Four things the screen owes the person holding it: which number it went to (so a wrong number is caught here, not after three failed tries), how long it lasts, when they may ask for another, and a plain warning that nobody from the shop will ever ring and ask for it.

No fake keyboard is drawn. The real one renders on top, and a painted one reads as a toy.

A FAILURE NAMES ITSELF — IN INK

The house rule is that no failure may be silent: say what went wrong and how to fix it. So the wrong-PIN screen says which thing failed, how many tries remain, that the lock is fifteen minutes, and that the PIN already sent is still good for six and a half.

AND IT IS NOT RED. Oxide on this surface means money owed and nothing else — that is the whole value of having one colour with one meaning on a screen full of figures. An error marked in oxide would make "you owe" and "you mistyped" the same colour.

So the error is ink, in words, on the warm ground, inside a firm rule, directly above the boxes it is about. Placement and wording carry it. If that turns out to be too quiet in a real yard in real sunlight, the fix is a heavier rule or a larger mark — not spending the money colour.

A DOCUMENT, NOT A SCREEN

Charge and payment get their own columns here. The phone had to merge them into one signed column to fit; at this width the merge is a loss, because a bursar reconciles by reading DOWN a column.

The head block carries what a printed statement carries: who the account is, the terms, the limit, and the balance due — so a print-out is complete without the chrome around it.

Still no accent. The three actions are outlined. Nothing on this page acts on money.
Counter — a design language for the client side

WHAT THIS SURFACE IS

The staff app is a dense work console: steel chrome, 13px type, a hundred figures a screen. It is an instrument.

This is not that. This is the shop's counter, open at 22:00, and its whole job is TRUST — that the price you were quoted in July is the price you get in September, that your balance is not a surprise, and that nothing was hidden from you.

So the language is a well-printed statement of account, not an app: warm paper, hairlines, square corners, real typographic hierarchy, and figures that line up in a column.

Built from the ground up. It shares no tokens with index.html — deliberately, so a customer can never mistake this screen for a staff screen.

FOLLOWING AN ORDER, HONESTLY

The ladder is the app's own order stages in the customer's words: sent, confirmed, getting your goods, ready, on the way, invoiced.

TWO RULES DO THE WORK.

A stage that has not happened carries NO DATE. The books cannot derive when a lorry will leave, so the screen does not invent it — a promised day that slips costs more trust than a blank one ever did.

And it says WHICH LINE is holding things up, per item, because an order is not one thing. "The ridge caps are being collected today" is the honest version of a progress bar.

What it never says is WHERE they are being collected from. This is the single most tempting place in the whole product to name a supplier, and the language has nowhere to put one.

THE SYSTEM

Ground #F4F1EA warm linen · Paper #FFFFFF · Ink #1A1714 warm near-black · Second #6B635A · Meta #9A9187 · Rule #E3DDD3 · Firm rule #C7BFB2

Two accents, one meaning each, matched in lightness and chroma:
   #14594A verdigris — exactly two jobs: THE one filled action, and links. Nothing else. Not "good", not "in stock", not a payment received — those are ink, and the words carry them.
   #9B3A22 oxide — money owed. Nothing else, ever. Not a button, and not "out of stock".

The single tinted ground in the system is the advice block, which is why it reads as advice rather than decoration.

Type: Newsreader for every figure and display line (a printed-statement serif with real numerals); Public Sans for the interface. Not Inter, not Roboto, and deliberately not the staff app's Fraunces.

Ramp 11 / 13 / 15 body / 17 / 22 / 34 / 44.
Space 4 8 12 16 20 24 32 40. Radius 4 on controls, ZERO on sheets — paper has square corners. Tap 44 minimum, and that includes back arrows and the account chip.

Depth is hairlines. One shadow in the whole system: the basket bar, because it genuinely floats.

THE ONE DEVICE: the ledger row

No cards. No coloured left borders. Every list in this language is the same row — name and its basis on the left, figure right-aligned in tabular numerals, a hairline between, a FIRMER rule under a total.

That single device carries the catalogue, the basket, the order history and the statement, on the phone and at 1440 alike. Four screens, one vocabulary, and it is exactly how a paper statement already works — which is the point: the customer has read this document before.

THE WORKFLOW LAW

One screen, one question, one action.

· The screen title IS the question it answers.
· Exactly one FILLED verdigris action, pinned at the bottom in the thumb, on every screen. Zero is allowed (see the Statement); two is a bug. Secondary acts are outlined in ink, never in the accent.
· Ordering is four named steps — Browse · How many · Check · Send — and the step line is drawn ONLY inside that flow.
· The customer never types a price, a code, or an address they have already given.

DERIVED, NEVER INVENTED — and the basis is SHOWN

The house rule says every figure comes from the books. This surface adds the harder half: the customer must be able to redo the arithmetic.

So the catalogue says 48,500 per sheet AND 51,000 loose, because 48,500 is the bundle price and a customer buying six sheets would otherwise have been quoted one figure and charged another. The nails say 1,120 at 8 a sheet AND about 11.2kg at 100 nails to the kg, because they are priced by weight and ordered by count. The over-limit line names the 1,240,000 already owed rather than quietly assuming zero.

Every one of those was wrong in the first draft, and each was wrong in the same way: the figure was right and its basis was invisible.

WHERE THE PRICE GATE SITS

Sign in carries no price at all, and offers the public catalogue by name: "Browse what we stock — names and photographs only. Prices are for account holders."

Everything from screen 3 onwards shows money, because by then we know exactly who is reading. And the figure is THEIRS — held from the last time we quoted them — so a leaked screenshot is one customer's number, not the price book.

No screen in this language has a place to put a supplier's name. That is a constraint of the design, not only of the data.

THE LINE BECOMES A LIST

The green block on screen 5 is the whole commercial argument in one component: "140 sheets takes about 1,120 roofing nails at 8 a sheet."

A supplier sells a line. This turns the line into a LIST — and a list is the thing one supplier cannot fill. It is the only tinted ground in the system, which is why it reads as advice.

Its Add button is OUTLINED, not verdigris. It is a real act, but it is not the act this screen is for, and two accent buttons competing for one thumb is how a screen stops having a primary action.

NO ACCENT ON THIS SCREEN

A statement is read, not acted on, so both buttons are outlined and the accent budget goes unspent. That is deliberate, not an oversight.

The closing figure is oxide because it is money owed. The footnote invites a customer to challenge a line before it becomes a dispute — the staff app already refuses to hide a disagreement between the debt log and the balance, and this is the customer-facing half of that same rule.
Not enough is an answer

A NEW ACCOUNT IS NOT A BROKEN ONE

The house rule: a strip reading 0, 0, 0 makes a working app look broken. Each tile says what it is WAITING FOR instead.

So day one does not show a 0 balance — it says "Nothing outstanding", and names the day the account was opened. Terms and limit ARE shown, because they are true from the first minute and they are the whole reason to have an account.

The long trading name in the chrome is deliberate: "Ssekitoleko Hardware" is the case the house truncation rule exists for, and it is here so the guard can be seen working rather than assumed.

AN EMPTY SEARCH IS A SALE

The public catalogue already refuses to say a flat "No products found" — it names WHICH cause, aisle or search, because the way out differs. The same rule here, and then one step further.

"We do not list it" is the single most valuable thing a customer can tell this shop. It is a demand signal, it is free, and the sourcing side already knows how to turn it into a product. So the accent on this screen is not "search again" — it is "Ask us to find gypsum board", with the honest promise a price and a lead time will come back.

The line about nine of the last ten is a claim the shop must actually be able to make. If it cannot, cut it — do not soften it.

THE ONE TRUE ROW

An empty statement still has an opening balance and a date, and both are facts. They stay.

No accent, exactly as on the full statement — a screen with nothing to act on must not grow a button to look finished.

The footnote offers to carry over trading history from before the account existed. That is not politeness: a customer who has bought from you for six years and sees a statement starting last Tuesday reads the portal as a downgrade.

STILL NOT DRAWN — say so rather than imply it is done

· The desktop half of the newer states: empty, tracking, cancelled, part supplied, and the people list.
· Adding somebody to an account, and the moment an approver sends an order back with a note.
· A delivery that is signed for short and then completed on a second lorry.

Sample figures are realistic but invented, and the arithmetic agrees across all twenty-seven artboards. One job runs through the LPO page, the phone flow and the people page: quotation QT-0417 at 19,112,640 before VAT, LPO/KPSS/2026/118 against it, delivery DN-2419 counted two ridge caps short, the purlins cancelled — and 16,978,595 invoiced.
If Counter is wrong, these are the other two

Both are drawn low-fi on purpose — they are here to settle a direction, not to be admired.

B · SHOPFRONT is the familiar one: cards, photo tiles, a bottom tab bar, the shape of every retail app your customers already use. Cheapest to get right, and nobody needs teaching. The cost is that it reads as a SHOP — the price becomes the hero, which invites the comparison you are trying not to invite, and the balance and terms become one card among cards.

C · CONSOLE hands the customer the staff app's own vocabulary. Zero new tokens, one system to maintain, and dense tables genuinely suit an institutional buyer. The cost is that it reads cold and administrative to a fundi standing in a yard, and a customer shown the staff chrome will assume they are seeing staff data.

Counter costs the most to build. It is the only one of the three whose shape argues that you are an account, not a price list.
The LPO path — where the price gate does not apply

THE ONE PLACE YOUR PRICES LEAVE THE BUILDING

Every other screen in this product keeps a price behind a verified login and shows a figure that is only that account's. An institutional quotation cannot do that. A school, an NGO or a district needs an itemised document, with unit prices, to put beside two other quotations. That is the procedure, and refusing it loses the work.

So do not pretend the gate holds here. Protect the margin with the things that actually protect it:

A VALIDITY DATE, stated twice and counted down. Fourteen days. After that you re-quote at the day's prices, and the document says so plainly rather than as small print. In a market where cement and steel move on the exchange rate, that single field is the difference between honouring a quote and eating one.

THE BASKET, NOT THE LINE. Delivery included, VAT shown, the whole job priced. A rival undercutting line three has still not quoted the job.

THE RELATIONSHIP. Terms, the promise not to substitute a make without asking, and a named person to ring. None of those appear on a price list.

WHAT A UGANDAN INSTITUTIONAL QUOTATION MUST CARRY

This is not a styled invoice. It is a procurement document, and a missing field gets it set aside rather than queried:

· Both TINs, and both addresses.
· A quotation number and a date, and the person it is addressed to by name and office.
· Unit, quantity, unit price and amount per line — no bundling, because the comparison is done line by line.
· VAT shown separately at 18%, never folded into the price.
· THE AMOUNT IN WORDS. It reads as a formality and it is not: it is what a cheque and an approval memo are written from.
· Terms, a validity date, and room for a signature and stamp.

The TINs and the shop address are left in brackets because they are yours and I do not have them. Everything else is drawn.

A CANCELLED ORDER IS A TRUST SCREEN

This is the screen a customer remembers. So it answers the three questions in order, and none of them is "sorry".

WHO cancelled it, and WHEN. Here it was the customer, at their word, after the shop rang — so both parties are named. A screen that says only "cancelled" invites the customer to assume you dropped them.

WHY, in the words a person would use: the valves could not be got at the price quoted, the only ones available were a different make and dearer, and the shop does not swap a make or lift a price without asking. That sentence is the entire argument for buying from you rather than from whoever answers the phone.

WHAT IT COST: nothing. Charged to your account, 0, under the firm rule and in full ink. What it WOULD have come to is kept, greyed, because a customer re-quoting wants to compare.

Then a way forward, and it is the accent. A dead end with no action is how an order becomes a lost customer.

The reason block is ink on the warm ground, not oxide — nothing is owed here, and oxide means money owed.

AN EXPIRY IS A CONVERSATION, NOT A DEAD END

The fourteen days are what protect the margin, so the screen has to honour them out loud: "those prices are no longer ours to give, and we will not pretend they are."

Then it does the useful thing. It says WHAT ACTUALLY MOVED — two lines of five, named, each carrying "was 48,500" beside today's figure, and the difference on the total. A customer who can see that three of their five lines have not moved in three weeks is looking at evidence that you price honestly, not at a shop that put its prices up because it could.

AND IT IS NOT A RE-QUOTE. A reading off the price registry is derived and fair to show; an offer is a document with a number, a signature and a fresh fourteen days. The screen says which of the two it is, and the accent is "Ask for a new quotation" — nothing re-quotes itself.
One account, several people, different powers

WHY THIS IS NOT A SETTINGS PAGE

A school, an NGO or a contractor is never one person. Somebody raises the order, somebody else approves it, and a third person stands at the gate when the lorry arrives. Give them one shared login and you get the worst of both: the storekeeper can see the negotiated rates, and nobody can prove who ordered what.

So the list is a CONTROL, and the screen says what the shop does with it rather than leaving it as configuration:

· An order over the approval figure does not reach the shop at all until the approver has said yes, on their own phone.
· An LPO signed by somebody not on the list is not accepted. If the signatory changes, it changes here first. That is the cheapest fraud control in the whole product.
· Removing somebody stops them seeing anything from that minute — and does NOT remove what they already ordered, which stays on the account under their name.

THE GATE, WORKING INSIDE AN ACCOUNT

Wasswa Peter receives goods and signs the delivery note. He sees no prices at all.

That is the same rule as the front door, one level in: a person needs what their job needs and no more. A storekeeper does not need the school's negotiated rates to count forty bags of cement against a note — and a storekeeper who has them is the likeliest route by which a rival learns what you charge this school.

It is also the answer to the objection that gating prices is unfriendly. It is not about trust. Sarah sees every figure. Peter has a different job.

THE APPROVER GETS A REASON, NOT JUST A FIGURE

The note from the person who raised it — "the term starts on the 14th and the carpenters want the purlins on site by Friday" — is the most important element on the screen. An approver handed a bare total rings back to ask why, and the order sits for two days.

Every line is shown, not three of five with a total. This is an approval: the whole list is the thing being approved.

Two acts, and only one is the accent. Approve sends it; sending it back to Sarah with a note is outlined, because the screen exists to get a decision, not to make refusing easy.

And the honest line at the foot: nothing reaches the shop until you approve it. Nothing sends itself, and the customer's own staff are no exception.

THE SCREEN WITH NO MONEY ON IT

Every other surface in this product is built around a figure. This one has none, and that is the test of whether the language generalises: the COUNT becomes the figure. Same serif, same tabular numerals, same right-hand column — 240, 46, 19.2, 40. Nothing else changed.

What the storekeeper is given is exactly what the job needs. What is meant to be on the lorry, what he counted, and what is short. The 46 sits where the money would be, and the two short are named in ink rather than hidden in a total.

THE TIMBER IS LISTED THOUGH IT IS NOT COMING. "Named rather than dropped" is a house rule and this is the case it was written for: a line silently missing from a delivery screen leaves a man standing at a gate waiting for a lorry that was cancelled a week ago.

And the screen says its own boundary out loud: you are signing for the count, this shows no prices, signing agrees to none. What is short reaches the shop and the bursar the moment he signs — not through him.

CHARGED FOR WHAT CAME, AND NOTHING ELSE

This is the same job as the quotation, the LPO and the delivery note, and it is where the whole canvas closes:

   supplied        14,388,640
   not supplied     4,724,000
                   ——————————
   the quotation   19,112,640

The purlins were cancelled because only 3m lengths could be got and the customer said not to substitute. Two ridge caps were short on the lorry and the storekeeper signed for 46. Neither is on the invoice, and the footnote does that subtraction where the customer can see it rather than leaving them to find it.

THE INVOICED FIGURE IS INK, NOT OXIDE. Oxide appears on exactly two screens in this product — Your account and the Statement — because that is where a balance lives. What an order was invoiced at is a record; whether it is owed is the statement's question. One colour, one meaning, and it does not wander.

The accent is the way forward: price the purlins again today. A part-supplied order with no next step is a customer going to find the timber somewhere else.
